# BLOC-BOT — Waffle Plate & Smart Block: CAD/Geometry Spec

Context: graduation project, master's electronics/embedded, Algeria. Report due 14 Oct 2026.
This is a design-in-progress handoff for CAD/scripting work (Fusion 360 export, OpenSCAD, or
STL generation/inspection). Treat FINAL as locked, PROPOSED as needing confirmation before
committing print time, and OPEN as undecided — don't invent a value for it.

## Plate

| Parameter | Value | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Material | PETG | FINAL |
| Large hole diameter | 6.0 mm | FINAL |
| Medium hole diameter | 4.5 mm | FINAL |
| Small hole diameter | 3.2 mm | FINAL |
| Large-hole fillet (top edge) | 0.75 mm | FINAL |
| Bottom-edge treatment | 45° chamfer, not a fillet (fillets on the unsupported bottom edge print as a bad overhang) | FINAL |
| Medium/small hole fillets | — | OPEN |
| Grid pitch | 10 mm proposed | PROPOSED — freeze before generating the full hole pattern |
| Plate outer size | 150–180 mm square | PROPOSED — driven by ~4h print time budget, not final dims |
| Plate thickness | — | OPEN |
| Number of plates | 2, stacked | FINAL |
| Plate spacing | M3 standoffs, 30–50 mm | PROPOSED |
| Print compensation | FDM holes print 0.1–0.3 mm undersized (elephant's foot worsens the bottom layer further) — oversize holes in CAD by this much, don't rely on nominal | FINAL (empirical rule, not measured on this plate yet) |

Lower plate carries motors (mounted via printed brackets using the SAME block footprint below —
not a bespoke mount), driver, battery, robot ESP32. Upper plate carries Smart Blocks only.

## Smart Block mounting — mechanical

**Decided approach:** blocks sit flat on the plate surface and bolt through the existing grid.
No peg-into-hole gripping — FDM hole tolerance is too loose and inconsistent to grip on reliably.

- One **universal 2-hole footprint** for every block type (sensor blocks AND motor brackets).
  Both holes are M3 clearance (3.2 mm), spaced at exactly the grid pitch so the footprint always
  lands on two adjacent grid holes.
- "8 directions" = 8 mounting **locations** spread around the plate perimeter (front, front-right,
  right, back-right, back, back-left, left, front-left) — NOT a rotating single block. This comes
  free from a full perimeter grid at the chosen pitch; no rotate/lock or pivot+slot mechanism needed.
- **OPEN — needs a decision in this session:** does a block need directional keying so a
  direction-sensitive sensor (e.g. HC-SR04, which must face outward to measure correctly) can't be
  bolted on backwards? Options to evaluate: asymmetric footprint (holes not mirror-symmetric),
  one clearance hole + one keyed/offset hole, or a small locating notch against a plate edge/rib.
  Pick whichever is simplest to print reliably at this scale — don't add mechanism for its own sake.
- Footprint should be small enough that adjacent perimeter positions don't foul each other at the
  chosen grid pitch — check this when the pitch is set.

## Electrical connector (for reference only, not a CAD constraint unless keying depends on it)

4-pin standard per block: 5V, GND, SDA/SIG1, SCL/SIG2. I2C blocks (MPU6050 etc.) use SDA/SCL;
simple blocks (HC-SR04 etc.) use the two signal pins as digital I/O.

## What I need from this session

1. Finalize grid pitch (10 mm proposed) and plate outer dimensions within the 150–180 mm target.
2. Design the universal block footprint: exact hole spacing, footprint outer size, and resolve the
   directional-keying question above.
3. Lay out the two-plate standoff positions (count and placement, not just length).
4. Once I have an STL, parse it (trimesh / numpy-stl) and report actual bounding box, hole
   diameters/positions, and manifold/watertight status — check these against the values above
   rather than assuming the CAD matches the spec.

## Do not invent

Final plate thickness, final medium/small fillet radii, final plate outer dimensions (only the
150–180 mm target range is set), final standoff count/positions, final footprint dimensions —
these are exactly what this session is for. Propose values and label them, don't assume them
as settled.

1	# BLOC-BOT — Working Context & Execution Plan (v1)
2	
3	**Prepared:** 9 September 2026
4	**Purpose:** Single file to upload at the start of any new conversation. Replaces the need to re-explain the project.
5	**Supersedes:** nothing. Sits alongside `Bloc-Bot_Critical_Prompts_Conversation_Transfer.docx` and `Bloc-Bot_Project_Detailed_Record.docx`.
6	
7	---
8	
9	## 0. READ THIS FIRST (instructions to the assistant)
10	
11	- Treat this document as project history and constraints, **not** as permission to invent missing specifications.
12	- Label every engineering statement as **FINAL**, **PROPOSED**, or **NEEDS TESTING**.
13	- The team is time-constrained and hardware-constrained. Prefer the boring, available, already-working option over the elegant one.
14	- Do not suggest anything that requires hardware they cannot buy in Sétif before ~23 September 2026.
15	- When they upload `.ino` / `.cpp` / `.h` files, that code is the source of truth and overrides this document.
16	
17	---
18	
19	## 1. WHO / WHAT / WHEN
20	
21	| Item | Value |
22	|---|---|
23	| Project | BLOC-BOT — open-source modular robotic platform ("living hardware breadboard") |
24	| Context | Master's graduation project, Electronics / Embedded Systems, Algeria |
25	| Team | Two people. **User** = controller side. **Friend** = robot side. |
26	| Hard deadline | **21 October 2026** (~6 weeks from 9 Sept) |
27	| Scope level | Undergraduate/master's demo standard. Not a research paper. Working demo + defensible report is the target. |
28	| Tooling | VS Code + PlatformIO, Fusion 360 |
29	| Gap | ~5 months of no activity. Both members need to re-familiarise. |
30	
31	### The dominating constraint
32	
33	**The user is physically in Sétif until roughly 23 September 2026 (~2 weeks).** After that:
34	
35	- No local electronics shops.
36	- Anything ordered costs money, takes ~2 days, and **cannot be exchanged or returned.**
37	- The friend, the 3D printer, and hands-on co-debugging are all in Sétif.
38	
39	Therefore: **all hardware acquisition, all hardware validation, and all physical printing must happen in the next two weeks.** Weeks 3–6 are firmware, integration-over-distance, documentation and report only.
40	
41	### Second constraint (often forgotten)
42	
43	The **report submission deadline is almost certainly earlier than 21 October** (typically 1–3 weeks before the defense). This must be confirmed with the supervisor immediately, because it compresses everything above.
44	
45	---
46	
47	## 2. CURRENT ASSET INVENTORY
48	
49	### Hardware in hand (user)
50	- 1 × ESP32 dev board
51	- 1 × small display (referred to as "LCD" — **must confirm whether it is a graphic OLED or a character LCD**; see §5.1). Planned upgrade to a larger screen.
52	- 1 × analog joystick module
53	- 1 × HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor
54	- 4–6 × pushbuttons
55	- Jumper wires
56	
57	### Hardware NOT yet acquired
58	Motors, wheels, motor driver, batteries, chargers, buck converter, second/third ESP32, breadboards, standoffs, screws, soldering equipment, multimeter (status unknown).
59	
60	### Software assets that already exist (written 7 Sept 2026, not yet hardware-validated)
61	| File | Status |
62	|---|---|
63	| `BLOC_BOT_Test_Firmware.ino` | Ready to run today. Tests joystick, buttons, HC-SR04, display. 4 test modes. |
64	| `BLOC_BOT_Controller.ino` | Written. Joystick calibration, deadzone, circular limit, OLED UI (Learner/Researcher), ESP-NOW TX/RX, battery monitor. Motor/battery sections commented out. |
65	| `BLOC_BOT_Robot.ino` | Written. PWM motor control, H-bridge direction, ESP-NOW RX/TX, HC-SR04, battery filter, 500 ms safety watchdog. Motor/battery sections commented out. |
66	
67	**None of the three has been validated against real hardware.** Treat all of it as NEEDS TESTING.
68	
69	---
70	
71	## 3. CONFIRMED PROJECT FACTS (do not re-litigate)
72	
73	| Area | Value | Status |
74	|---|---|---|
75	| Concept | Reconfigurable modular robot, perforated "Waffle Plate" mechanical standard | FINAL |
76	| Comms | ESP-NOW peer-to-peer, ESP32 ↔ ESP32 | FINAL |
77	| Controller display | 128×64 I2C graphic display, address 0x3C, SDA 21 / SCL 22 | FINAL (pending screen upgrade) |
78	| UI concept | Two modes: "Learner" (simple) and "Researcher" (telemetry) | FINAL |
79	| Waffle Plate material | PETG | FINAL |
80	| Hole diameters | 6.0 mm large / 4.5 mm medium / 3.2 mm small | FINAL |
81	| Large-hole fillet | 0.75 mm | FINAL |
82	| Joystick centre offsets | X = +11, Y = −12 (measured ADC units) | FINAL (measured) |
83	| Circular drive limit | Vector normalisation, clamp magnitude to radius, preserve direction | FINAL (behaviour) |
84	| Motor performance target | Human walking pace. Not a racing robot. | FINAL (design intent) |
85	| Development philosophy | Design → Build → Test → Modify → Retest | FINAL |
86	| Print workflow | Fusion 360 → STL → friend's slicer → Ender → print | FINAL |
87	
88	---
89	
90	## 4. STILL OPEN (do not invent values for these)
91	
92	- Final Waffle Plate outer dimensions, thickness, grid pitch
93	- Medium-hole and small-hole fillet radii
94	- Motor model, wheel diameter, gear ratio
95	- Motor driver model (DRV8833 / L293D / L298N / TB6612 all discussed, none chosen)
96	- Battery configuration (proposal said 3S/4S; later discussion considered lower voltage — **unresolved**)
97	- Ultrasonic mounting position and validated GPIO assignment
98	- Whether the "Smart Block" module standard is a deliverable or just a documented concept
99	
100	---
101	
102	## 5. DECISIONS TO MAKE THIS WEEK (all PROPOSED — confirm or replace, then freeze)
103	
104	### 5.1 Display — the drive-circle UI requires a *graphic* display
105	
106	A 16×2 or 20×4 character LCD **cannot draw the circular drive indicator**, which is one of the project's distinguishing features. If the current screen is a character LCD, it must be replaced.
107	
108	| Option | Notes |
109	|---|---|
110	| 1.3" SH1106 I2C OLED | Drop-in bigger version of the 0.96" SSD1306. With the U8g2 library, changing screens = changing one constructor line. Lowest-risk upgrade. |
111	| 2.42" SSD1309 I2C/SPI OLED | Much more visible during a defense. Same monochrome code. |
112	| 2.4"/2.8" ILI9341 SPI TFT (colour) | Biggest visual impact for the jury. Requires TFT_eSPI or LovyanGFX and more wiring. Higher risk, higher reward. |
113	
114	**Recommendation:** buy **both** a 1.3" SH1106 *and* a 2.4" ILI9341 while in Sétif. They are cheap, and there is no second chance to buy. Develop against the SH1106 (safe), and switch to the TFT only if there is spare time in week 4.
115	
116	**Also:** migrate display code from Adafruit_SSD1306 to **U8g2** now. It supports SSD1306, SH1106, SSD1309 and more behind one API, which makes the screen upgrade a one-line change instead of a rewrite.
117	
118	### 5.2 Motors — buy geared motors and delete the gear-reduction problem
119	
120	The old record spends effort on pulley reduction, printed gears and friction wheels. **Do not build a custom reduction.** Buy motors with a gearbox already attached. This removes an entire mechanical sub-project.
121	
122	| Option | Notes |
123	|---|---|
124	| "Yellow" TT gearmotor, 1:48, 3–6 V | Ubiquitous, cheap, comes with matching wheels. ~150 mA free-run, ~1 A stall at 6 V. Perfect for human-pace. Sloppy plastic gearbox, no encoder. |
125	| N20 metal gearmotor, 6 V or 12 V, ~100–300 RPM | Small, much better quality, optional encoder version. Needs mounting brackets. |
126	
127	**Recommendation:** buy **4 × TT gearmotors + 4 wheels** (2 spare) as the guaranteed-working baseline, and **2 × N20 with encoders** if available and affordable, as an upgrade path. Buy a caster ball for the third contact point.
128	
129	### 5.3 Motor driver — decide by measurement, buy by availability
130	
131	The rule from the existing record still holds: measure stall current before committing. But the practical answer is to buy more than one, because you cannot come back.
132	
133	| Driver | Max continuous | Notes |
134	|---|---|---|
135	| L298N module | ~2 A/ch | Universally available in Algeria. Inefficient, drops ~1.8–2 V, gets hot, needs heatsink. Works fine with TT motors. |
136	| DRV8833 module | ~1.5 A/ch | Efficient, low voltage drop, 2.7–10.8 V. Best match for TT motors on 2S. |
137	| TB6612FNG module | ~1.2 A/ch | The sweet spot. Efficient, small, robust. |
138	
139	**Recommendation:** buy **L298N (guaranteed) + DRV8833 or TB6612FNG (preferred)**. All three are pin-compatible with the existing robot firmware's IN1/IN2 + PWM logic.
140	
141	### 5.4 Battery — simplify to 2S, and justify the deviation in the report
142	
143	The 3S/4S concept in the original proposal was written before motor selection. If the motors are 6 V TT gearmotors, 3S/4S is wrong.
144	
145	**Proposed architecture:**
146	```
147	2 × 18650 in series (2S, 7.4 V nominal, 8.4 V full)
148	  → 2S BMS protection board
149	  → motor driver (motors see ~5.6-6.5V through an L298N, or ~7V through a DRV8833)
150	  → MP1584 or LM2596 buck converter → 5 V → ESP32 VIN
151	  → voltage divider → GPIO 36 for battery telemetry
152	```
153	This is simpler, safer, cheaper and easier to defend than 4S. **Document the change and the reason** — a deliberate, justified deviation from the proposal reads as engineering maturity in a defense. An unexplained one reads as drift.
154	
155	Buy: 4 × 18650 cells, 2 × 2S BMS, 2 × buck converters, 1 × 18650 charger, 1 × 2S battery holder. Plus a **multimeter** if you don't own one — non-negotiable.
156	
157	### 5.5 Buy multiple ESP32 boards. This is the single highest-value purchase.
158	
159	**You currently have one ESP32. ESP-NOW requires two. You cannot test the core feature of your project.**
160	
161	Buy **4 × ESP32 DevKit V1 (30-pin WROOM-32)**:
162	- 1 = your controller
163	- 1 = your desk stand-in for the robot (so you can develop ESP-NOW alone, from home, after leaving Sétif)
164	- 1 = friend's robot
165	- 1 = spare (boards die, USB ports break, regulators blow)
166	
167	Also buy **3 × known-good USB data cables**. A charge-only cable that doesn't enumerate has cost more student hours than any other single failure.
168	
169	---
170	
171	## 6. PROPOSED PIN MAP (v1 — freeze after validation)
172	
173	### Critical ESP32 rules that constrain this
174	1. **ADC2 pins (GPIO 0, 2, 4, 12–15, 25–27) do not work while WiFi/ESP-NOW is active.** All analog inputs must be on **ADC1: GPIO 32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 39.** The existing code already gets this right.
175	2. **GPIO 34–39 are input-only and have no internal pull-ups.** Fine for analog, unusable for buttons without external resistors.
176	3. **Strapping pins (0, 2, 5, 12, 15) affect boot.** GPIO 12 pulled HIGH at boot = **board fails to boot**. See §7 bug list.
177	
178	### Controller (user)
179	| Function | GPIO | Note |
180	|---|---|---|
181	| Joystick VRx | 34 | ADC1, input-only |
182	| Joystick VRy | 35 | ADC1, input-only |
183	| Joystick SW | 32 | INPUT_PULLUP, active low |
184	| Display SDA | 21 | I2C |
185	| Display SCL | 22 | I2C |
186	| Button 1 | 33 | INPUT_PULLUP |
187	| Button 2 | 25 | INPUT_PULLUP |
188	| Button 3 | 26 | INPUT_PULLUP |
189	| Button 4 | 27 | INPUT_PULLUP |
190	| Button 5 | 14 | INPUT_PULLUP |
191	| Button 6 | **13** | INPUT_PULLUP — **moved off GPIO 12, see §7** |
192	| Controller battery sense | 36 | ADC1, via divider |
193	
194	### Robot (friend)
195	| Function | GPIO | Note |
196	|---|---|---|
197	| Left motor PWM | 19 | moved off GPIO 5 (strapping pin) |
198	| Right motor PWM | 23 | |
199	| Left IN1 / IN2 | 25 / 26 | |
200	| Right IN1 / IN2 | 27 / 14 | |
201	| Ultrasonic TRIG | 5 | output only, safe |
202	| Ultrasonic ECHO | 18 | **via 1 kΩ / 2 kΩ divider, see §7** |
203	| Battery sense | 36 | ADC1, via divider |
204	
205	---
206	
207	## 7. BUGS AND HAZARDS IN THE EXISTING FIRMWARE (fix before first power-on)
208	
209	1. **`BTN_6_PIN = 12` will prevent the board from booting.** GPIO 12 (MTDI) is sampled at reset to select flash voltage. `INPUT_PULLUP` holds it high, which selects 1.8 V and bricks the boot. **Move button 6 to GPIO 13.**
210	
211	2. **HC-SR04 ECHO outputs 5 V into a 3.3 V pin.** The ESP32 is not 5 V tolerant. Add a divider on ECHO: 1 kΩ from ECHO to the GPIO, 2 kΩ from the GPIO to GND. (Alternative: buy an RCWL-1601 / HC-SR04+, which is 3.3 V safe. Buy one while in Sétif as a backup.) Note that HC-SR04 still needs **5 V on VCC** to work reliably.
212	
213	3. **`pulseIn` timeout of 60 ms blocks the whole loop.** The robot claims 20 Hz telemetry (50 ms budget) but a missing echo stalls for 60 ms, so the watchdog timing and telemetry rate become unreliable. Reduce the timeout to **25 ms** (≈4.3 m, beyond the sensor's useful range anyway) and only ping every 100 ms rather than every loop.
214	
215	4. **RSSI is a hard-coded placeholder (−50 dBm).** It displays a fabricated number as measured telemetry. In a defense this is a serious credibility problem if noticed. Either extract real RSSI, or replace it with **packet loss % and link latency**, computed from a sequence counter in the packet. Packet loss is a better link-quality metric anyway and is trivial to compute.
216	
217	5. **I2C is at the default 100 kHz.** A full 128×64 frame is 1024 bytes ≈ 100 ms at 100 kHz, which saturates the claimed 10 Hz display rate and blocks everything else. Add `Wire.setClock(400000);` in setup.
218	
219	6. **`BATTERY_DIVIDER` is 2 on the controller and 3 on the robot**, both placeholders. Measure the actual resistors and verify against a multimeter. Also note the ESP32 ADC is non-linear near the rails; keep the divided voltage between roughly 0.3 V and 2.8 V.
220	
221	7. **GPIO 5 as motor PWM** is a strapping pin that must be high at boot; some boards output a PWM pulse on it during boot. With a motor driver attached this can cause a brief unexpected motor twitch on power-up. Moved to GPIO 19 in the map above.
222	
223	8. **The controller computes `motor_left` / `motor_right` and sends those.** This works, but it means the robot cannot change its own mixing or apply obstacle-avoidance overrides cleanly. Consider sending `x`, `y` and letting the robot mix. **Low priority — only if time allows.** Do not refactor this in week 5.
224	
225	---
226	
227	## 8. THE SHARED PROTOCOL HEADER (highest-value software decision)
228	
229	Because the two of you will be **geographically separated during integration**, the link between the two firmwares must be frozen in a single shared file, committed to git, that both projects `#include`. Once this exists, each of you can develop independently against a stub of the other side.
230	
231	Create `include/blocbot_protocol.h`, identical in both PlatformIO projects:
232	
233	```cpp
234	#pragma once
235	#include <stdint.h>
236	
237	#define BLOCBOT_PROTO_VERSION 1
238	
239	enum : uint8_t { MSG_DRIVE = 1, MSG_TELEMETRY = 2 };
240	
241	typedef struct __attribute__((packed)) {
242	  uint8_t  version;      // BLOCBOT_PROTO_VERSION
243	  uint8_t  type;         // MSG_DRIVE
244	  uint16_t seq;          // increments every packet, wraps
245	  int16_t  motor_left;   // -255..+255
246	  int16_t  motor_right;  // -255..+255
247	  uint8_t  mode;         // 0 = Learner, 1 = Researcher
248	  uint8_t  buttons;      // bitfield, b0..b5
249	  uint8_t  estop;        // 1 = stop immediately
250	  uint8_t  reserved;
251	} DriveCmd;              // 12 bytes
252	
253	typedef struct __attribute__((packed)) {
254	  uint8_t  version;
255	  uint8_t  type;         // MSG_TELEMETRY
256	  uint16_t seq;          // echoes the last DriveCmd.seq received
257	  int16_t  motor_left;   // actually applied
258	  int16_t  motor_right;
259	  uint16_t battery_mv;
260	  uint16_t distance_cm;  // 0xFFFF = invalid / no echo
261	  int8_t   rssi;         // real value, or omit this field
262	  uint8_t  flags;        // b0 paired, b1 watchdog tripped, b2 obstacle, b3 low batt
263	  uint16_t uptime_s;
264	} Telemetry;             // 18 bytes
265	```
266	
267	The `seq` field is what makes real link telemetry possible: the controller knows how many commands it sent and how many were echoed back, so **packet loss %** and **round-trip latency in ms** both fall out for free. That is a far stronger thing to show a jury than a fake RSSI number.
268	
269	### Stub firmwares (build these in week 1)
270	- `stub_robot.ino` — receives `DriveCmd`, prints it, replies with plausible `Telemetry` (fake battery ramp, fake distance sweep). Lets the **user** develop and demo the full controller UI alone, from home, with no robot.
271	- `stub_controller.ino` — sends a scripted `DriveCmd` sequence. Lets the **friend** test motors and the watchdog with no controller.
272	
273	Once these exist, the 2-week separation stops being a project risk.
274	
275	---
276	
277	## 9. THE PLAN (6 weeks, worked backwards from 21 October)
278	
279	### Week 1 — 9–16 Sept · **SÉTIF · BUY AND VALIDATE**
280	Highest priority week of the entire project.
281	
282	- [ ] **Day 1:** confirm the real report submission deadline with the supervisor.
283	- [ ] **Day 1:** create the git repo. Push both firmwares as-is, before changing anything.
284	- [ ] **Day 1–3: shop.** Full list in §10. Buy spares of everything.
285	- [ ] Fix the GPIO 12 boot bug and the ECHO divider (§7) before first power-on.
286	- [ ] Run `BLOC_BOT_Test_Firmware.ino` on the bench. Validate: joystick raw values, re-measure centre offsets (the +11/−12 may have drifted or belong to a different unit), all buttons, HC-SR04 distance sweep, display.
287	- [ ] Bring up the second ESP32 and get **ESP-NOW talking in both directions**. This is the project's spine.
288	- [ ] Write `blocbot_protocol.h` and both stub firmwares.
289	- [ ] Measure motor stall current with the multimeter. Lock the driver choice.
290	- [ ] **Freeze the Waffle Plate CAD.** Record every dimension: outer size, thickness, grid pitch, hole pattern, fillets.
291	- [ ] Print the **test coupon** first (§11), not the full plate.
292	
293	### Week 2 — 17–23 Sept · **SÉTIF · BUILD AND SPLIT**
294	- [ ] Measure the test coupon. Correct hole diameters for shrinkage. Re-print if needed.
295	- [ ] Print the full Waffle Plate.
296	- [ ] Assemble the robot chassis: motors, wheels, caster, driver, battery, ESP32.
297	- [ ] Bench-test the robot with wheels off the ground: drive commands, direction, watchdog, ultrasonic, battery telemetry.
298	- [ ] **First end-to-end test: real controller → ESP-NOW → real robot → motors turning.** Even if ugly, get this to happen before you leave.
299	- [ ] **Record a video of it working.** This is your insurance policy.
300	- [ ] **Split the hardware.** User takes: controller + spare ESP32 (stub robot) + spare display + spare joystick + buttons + a spare HC-SR04. Friend takes: robot + spare ESP32 + spare motors + spare driver.
301	- [ ] **LAST SHOPPING DAY. Walk the shops one final time and buy anything you are even slightly unsure about.**
302	- [ ] Agree the integration meeting date (see risk in §12).
303	
304	### Week 3 — 24–30 Sept · **APART · PARALLEL DEVELOPMENT**
305	- **User:** finish the Learner UI (circular indicator, connection status, battery). Finish the Researcher UI (packet loss %, latency, battery, distance, raw commands). Migrate to U8g2. Bring up the larger screen. Test everything against `stub_robot`.
306	- **Friend:** finish chassis mechanics, cable management, mount the Waffle Plate, tune motor deadband and PWM curve, test against `stub_controller`. Print any brackets or module blocks.
307	- **Both:** daily push to git. Commit `blocbot_protocol.h` changes only by agreement.
308	- **Both:** start the report. Write the sections you can already write (introduction, state of the art, proposal recap, CAD chapter, protocol chapter). Do not leave this to week 5.
309	
310	### Week 4 — 1–7 Oct · **INTEGRATION**
311	- [ ] Physical integration session (in person if at all possible, see §12).
312	- [ ] Full system test: drive, telemetry, watchdog, mode switching, obstacle stop.
313	- [ ] Run the formal test sequence from §11 and **record results in a table**. Empty pass/fail tables are what separate a documented project from a demo.
314	- [ ] **Feature freeze at the end of this week.** Nothing new after 7 October.
315	
316	### Week 5 — 8–14 Oct · **DOCUMENT AND DE-RISK**
317	- [ ] Finish the report. Figures, wiring diagram, CAD renders, test result tables, photos.
318	- [ ] **Record a full, clean demo video.** If the live demo fails on the day, you play this. Every experienced team does this.
319	- [ ] Prepare the slide deck.
320	- [ ] Publish the GitHub repo properly: README, wiring diagram, `blocbot_protocol.h` spec, Waffle Plate STL + dimensioned drawing, licence (MIT for code, CERN-OHL-S or CC-BY-SA 4.0 for hardware). **This is your "open-source" objective made real, and it takes about two hours.**
321	- [ ] Charge every battery. Pack every spare.
322	
323	### Week 6 — 15–21 Oct · **REHEARSE AND DEFEND**
324	- [ ] Rehearse the demo at least five times, including deliberately unplugging things.
325	- [ ] Rehearse the presentation out loud, timed.
326	- [ ] Prepare answers for the likely questions (§13).
327	- [ ] Build the demo kit: robot, controller, charged spares, spare ESP32s pre-flashed, USB cables, laptop with PlatformIO working offline, the video on a USB stick.
328	- [ ] **No code changes in the final 48 hours.**
329	
330	---
331	
332	## 10. SÉTIF SHOPPING LIST (buy in the next 3 days)
333	
334	**Rule: for anything under a few hundred dinars that the project depends on, buy two.** You cannot come back.
335	
336	### Non-negotiable
337	- [ ] 4 × ESP32 DevKit V1 (30-pin, WROOM-32)
338	- [ ] 3 × USB data cables (verify each one enumerates before leaving the shop)
339	- [ ] 1 × digital multimeter (if you don't own one)
340	- [ ] 4 × TT gearmotors + 4 × wheels + 1 × caster ball
341	- [ ] 1 × L298N **and** 1 × DRV8833 or TB6612FNG
342	- [ ] 4 × 18650 cells + 2 × 2S BMS + 1 × charger + 2 × 2S holders
343	- [ ] 2 × buck converters (MP1584 or LM2596)
344	- [ ] 1 × 1.3" SH1106 I2C OLED (and a 2.4" ILI9341 TFT if affordable)
345	- [ ] 2 × analog joystick modules
346	- [ ] 2 × HC-SR04 (plus 1 × RCWL-1601 if available)
347	- [ ] 10 × tactile buttons
348	- [ ] 2 × solderless breadboards
349	- [ ] Male-male, male-female, female-female jumper wires (a full pack of each)
350	- [ ] Resistor assortment (must include 1 kΩ, 2 kΩ, 10 kΩ, 100 kΩ)
351	
352	### Strongly recommended
353	- [ ] Soldering iron, solder, flux, desoldering wick
354	- [ ] M3 screws (8/10/12/16 mm), M3 nuts, M3 nylon standoffs, M4 screws and nuts
355	- [ ] Heat-shrink tubing, electrical tape, zip ties
356	- [ ] Perfboard / stripboard (2 pieces)
357	- [ ] A rocker or slide power switch (2)
358	- [ ] Small screwdriver set, wire strippers, side cutters
359	- [ ] Spare PETG filament in the same colour as the plate print
360	
361	---
362	
363	## 11. TESTING
364	
365	### 11.1 Print test coupon (before the full plate)
366	Print a **60 × 60 mm** square of the Waffle Plate at the real thickness, containing at least two of each hole size. This costs ~15 minutes of print time and saves a failed 6-hour print.
367	
368	Measure with calipers:
369	- Actual vs nominal hole diameters. FDM holes print **undersized by roughly 0.1–0.3 mm** because of extrusion overlap. If the 3.2 mm hole measures 3.0 mm, an M3 screw will not pass. Compensate in CAD, don't drill.
370	- Elephant's foot on the first layer shrinks bottom-of-hole diameters further.
371	- Flatness and warping.
372	
373	**Fillet note:** the 0.75 mm fillet works on the *top* edge of a hole. On the *bottom* edge, resting on the build plate, a fillet becomes an unsupported overhang and prints badly. Use a **45° chamfer** on the bottom edge instead of a fillet. This is also probably the real cause of the Fusion 360 fillet error recorded earlier: an over-large radius on geometry too thin to support it.
374	
375	### 11.2 Formal test sequence
376	For every test, record: **objective / setup / procedure / expected / actual / pass-fail / cause if failed / action**. Fill this in as you go and paste it into the report.
377	
378	| # | Test | Pass criterion |
379	|---|---|---|
380	| T01 | Joystick raw range | X and Y sweep full 0–4095, centre stable within ±20 |
381	| T02 | Centre calibration | Calibrated output = 0 ± deadzone when untouched, for 60 s |
382	| T03 | Circular limit | Full diagonal deflection produces magnitude = radius, not radius × √2 |
383	| T04 | Button matrix | All 6 register, no ghosting, no bounce over 100 presses |
384	| T05 | HC-SR04 accuracy | Measured vs tape measure at 10/25/50/100/200 cm, error < 5 % |
385	| T06 | HC-SR04 out of range | Returns invalid, does not return 0 cm or stall the loop |
386	| T07 | ESP-NOW link | 1000 packets sent, loss < 1 % at 1 m |
387	| T08 | ESP-NOW range | Loss vs distance at 1/5/10/20/30 m, indoors and outdoors |
388	| T09 | Latency | Round-trip from seq echo, median and worst case |
389	| T10 | Safety watchdog | Power off the controller mid-drive; motors stop within 500 ms |
390	| T11 | Battery telemetry | Reported mV within 3 % of multimeter across the discharge range |
391	| T12 | Motor stall current | Measured with wheels blocked; below the driver's continuous rating |
392	| T13 | Drive straightness | Robot tracks straight over 3 m with equal commands, or deviation is documented |
393	| T14 | Runtime | Continuous driving until low-battery cutoff, minutes recorded |
394	| T15 | Waffle Plate fit | M3/M4 hardware passes all holes without forcing |
395	| T16 | Module swap | A block is removed and re-mounted in a different position in under 60 s |
396	
397	T07, T08, T09 and T10 are the ones that make this an *embedded systems* project rather than a toy. Prioritise them.
398	
399	---
400	
401	## 12. RISK REGISTER
402	
403	| Risk | Impact | Mitigation |
404	|---|---|---|
405	| **Report deadline is earlier than 21 Oct** | Loses 1–3 weeks | Confirm with supervisor on day 1 |
406	| **You and the friend are apart during integration** | Highest structural risk | Shared protocol header + stub firmwares (§8). Plan a physical integration meeting in week 4 **now**, and book travel. |
407	| Component fails after you leave Sétif | Days lost to shipping, or dead project | Buy doubles of everything (§10) |
408	| Waffle Plate print fails or fits wrong | Mechanical work stalls | Test coupon first (§11.1) |
409	| Live demo fails during defense | Catastrophic on the day | Pre-recorded demo video + pre-flashed spare boards |
410	| Motor stall current exceeds the driver | Driver dies mid-project | Measure in week 1, buy two driver types |
411	| Scope creep (Smart Blocks, ROS, camera, app) | Runs out the clock | **Feature freeze 7 October.** Anything not started by then becomes "Future Work" in the report, which is a legitimate chapter. |
412	| 5-month knowledge gap | Slow restart | Re-run the test firmware first. Reading your own working code is the fastest way to remember. |
413	
414	**On scope:** it is far better to defend a modest robot that provably works, with a complete test log and honest documentation, than an ambitious one that doesn't. Every unfinished feature you cut becomes a "Future Work" bullet, and juries reward a clear-eyed roadmap.
415	
416	---
417	
418	## 13. LIKELY DEFENSE QUESTIONS — prepare answers now
419	
420	1. Why ESP-NOW instead of WiFi, Bluetooth or LoRa? (Answer: connectionless, ~1–2 ms latency, no AP needed, 250-byte payload is sufficient, peer-to-peer. Have measured latency numbers ready.)
421	2. What happens if the wireless link drops mid-drive? (Answer: 500 ms watchdog, motors stop. **Demonstrate it live.**)
422	3. Why did you deviate from the 3S/4S battery in the proposal? (Answer: motor voltage rating drove the change. Show the calculation.)
423	4. Why PETG and not PLA or ABS? (Impact resistance, layer adhesion, less brittle than PLA, easier than ABS, no enclosure needed.)
424	5. Why three hole sizes? (M3 clearance = 3.2 mm, M4 clearance = 4.5 mm, 6.0 mm for standoffs and cable routing. Say exactly this.)
425	6. What is your grid pitch and why? (You must decide and be able to justify it. A 10 mm pitch is clean, metric and compatible with M3/M4 hardware.)
426	7. How does another person build a compatible module? (Point at the published repo and the dimensioned drawing. This is where the open-source objective gets its marks.)
427	8. What is the measured range and packet loss? (Have the T08 table ready.)
428	9. What would you do differently with more time? (Encoders and closed-loop speed control, IMU, PCB instead of jumper wires, more sensor blocks.)
429	10. Which parts are your own work and which are libraries? (Be honest and specific. This question is asked more often than students expect.)
430	
431	---
432	
433	## 14. HOW TO GET THE MOST OUT OF THE ASSISTANT
434	
435	**Do:**
436	- Keep everything in this Claude Project. Upload this file at the start of any long new conversation.
437	- Upload **actual code files**, not screenshots of code.
438	- Use **one conversation per work-stream**: CAD, controller firmware, robot firmware, report. Long mixed threads degrade.
439	- When debugging, give: exact serial output, exact compiler error, what you expected, and what changed since it last worked.
440	- Ask for a **decision rule**, not an opinion: "give me a rule for choosing between DRV8833 and L298N based on a measurement I can take" beats "which is better".
441	- Say **"this is FINAL"** when something is decided, so alternatives stop being offered.
442	- Ask for the report chapter as soon as a subsystem works, while the details are fresh.
443	- Ask it to play **hostile examiner** and grill you before the defense. Do this at least twice.
444	- Photos of wiring work well. So do photos of the Fusion 360 screen when a feature fails.
445	- Ask for **files**: BOM spreadsheet, test-result sheet, report skeleton, wiring table. It can generate .docx, .xlsx, .pdf and .md directly.
446	
447	**Don't:**
448	- Don't ask it to invent a dimension, GPIO, part number or packet format that hasn't been decided. Ask it to *propose* one and label it.
449	- Don't paste a 900-line file and say "fix it". Say what's broken.
450	- Don't accept a code rewrite of working firmware. Ask for a **diff-style explanation** of what changes and why.
451	- Don't ask it to design your whole report in week 6. Build it incrementally from week 3.
452	- Don't let it talk you into a feature. If it suggests something after 7 October, the answer is "Future Work".
453	
454	**Useful reusable prompts:**
455	- *"Here is my current controller code. Before suggesting anything, tell me what it does, in order. Then list what you would change and why, ranked by risk. Change nothing yet."*
456	- *"I measured X. Given the plan in the context file, does this change any FINAL decision?"*
457	- *"Write the test procedure for T0n in the standard format. Leave the actual-result column blank."*
458	- *"Act as my defense jury. Ask me five hard questions about the wireless link, then critique my answers."*
459	- *"Turn this week's engineering log into a report section, in formal academic French/English, with a figure list."*
460	
461	---
462	
463	## 15. LEARNING RESOURCES
464	
465	Verify anything version-sensitive against the official docs; tutorials age badly.
466	
467	### ESP32 / ESP-NOW / firmware
468	- **Random Nerd Tutorials** (randomnerdtutorials.com) — the canonical ESP32 reference. Their two-way ESP-NOW guide is the exact pattern this project uses. Also good on ESP32 ADC quirks and OLED.
469	- **Espressif official docs** (docs.espressif.com) — ESP-NOW API, and the ADC2/WiFi conflict is documented here. Cite this in the report rather than a blog.
470	- **DroneBot Workshop** (YouTube) — long, careful videos on L298N, DRV8833, TB6612, HC-SR04 and ESP-NOW. Best single channel for this project.
471	- **Andreas Spiess** (YouTube) — ESP-NOW range and power measurement, done experimentally. Directly relevant to your "Researcher" telemetry mode and to test T08.
472	- **Paul McWhorter** (YouTube) — very slow, very complete ESP32/Arduino series. Good for the 5-month re-entry problem.
473	- **Electronoobs**, **GreatScott!** (YouTube) — motor drivers, buck converters, battery packs.
474	- **U8g2 wiki** (github.com/olikraus/u8g2) — the display library to migrate to.
475	- **Bodmer / TFT_eSPI** (github.com/Bodmer/TFT_eSPI) — if you go with the colour TFT.
476	
477	### Fusion 360 / design for 3D printing
478	- **Product Design Online** (Kevin Kennedy, YouTube) — the best free structured Fusion 360 course. Start with his beginner series.
479	- **Lars Christensen** (YouTube) — more advanced Fusion 360.
480	- **CNC Kitchen** (Stefan Hermann, YouTube) — empirical tests on hole tolerance, print orientation vs strength, and infill. Directly applicable to the Waffle Plate, and quotable in the report because he publishes methodology.
481	- **Slant 3D** (YouTube) — design-for-printing rules, including why chamfers beat fillets on bottom edges.
482	- **Teaching Tech** (YouTube) — Ender calibration and first-layer setup, for your friend.
483	
484	### Inspiration and prior art (cite these in the report's state-of-the-art chapter)
485	- **TurtleBot3 (Burger / Waffle)** — ROBOTIS. Almost certainly the ancestor of your "Waffle Plate" name. Perforated modular plate chassis, extremely well documented at emanual.robotis.com. **Your single most useful comparison point.**
486	- **GoBILDA** — a commercial modular robotics ecosystem built on a strict 8 mm hole grid. Excellent justification material for choosing a grid pitch.
487	- **Actobotics / ServoCity** — another grid-based modular hardware standard.
488	- **Makeblock mBot / mBot Ranger** — modular beams plus standardised module ports. Their "module" abstraction is close to your Smart Blocks concept.
489	- **LEGO Technic** — the original 8 mm modular grid. Worth one paragraph on why standardised pitch enables an ecosystem.
490	- **OpenBot** (Intel Intelligent Systems Lab, GitHub) — open-source robot with exemplary repo structure and documentation. Copy their README organisation.
491	- **Poppy Project** — open-source modular robotics with a strong documentation and community model.
492	- **Thymio II** — educational robot with a genuinely well-designed simple UI. Good reference for your "Learner" mode.
493	- **Printables / Thingiverse** — search "modular robot chassis", "grid plate", "perfboard chassis" for mechanical ideas.
494	- **Hackaday.io** — browse project pages for the documentation format juries like.
495	
496	---
497	
498	## 16. CHANGE LOG
499	
500	| Date | Rev | Change | Reason |
501	|---|---|---|---|
502	| 2026-09-09 | v1 | Document created. Consolidated context, constraints, 6-week plan, shopping list, pin map, firmware bug list, protocol header, test plan, resources. | Project restart after ~5 months; hard deadline 21 Oct 2026; 2-week hardware window in Sétif. |
503	
504	---
505	*End of BLOC-BOT Working Context & Execution Plan v1*

# BLOC-BOT — Working Context & Execution Plan (v1)

**Prepared:** 9 September 2026
**Purpose:** Single file to upload at the start of any new conversation. Replaces the need to re-explain the project.
**Supersedes:** nothing. Sits alongside `Bloc-Bot_Critical_Prompts_Conversation_Transfer.docx` and `Bloc-Bot_Project_Detailed_Record.docx`.

---

## 0. READ THIS FIRST (instructions to the assistant)

- Treat this document as project history and constraints, **not** as permission to invent missing specifications.
- Label every engineering statement as **FINAL**, **PROPOSED**, or **NEEDS TESTING**.
- The team is time-constrained and hardware-constrained. Prefer the boring, available, already-working option over the elegant one.
- Do not suggest anything that requires hardware they cannot buy in Sétif before ~23 September 2026.
- When they upload `.ino` / `.cpp` / `.h` files, that code is the source of truth and overrides this document.

---

## 1. WHO / WHAT / WHEN

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Project | BLOC-BOT — open-source modular robotic platform ("living hardware breadboard") |
| Context | Master's graduation project, Electronics / Embedded Systems, Algeria |
| Team | Two people. **User** = controller side. **Friend** = robot side. |
| Hard deadline | **21 October 2026** (~6 weeks from 9 Sept) |

## 5. DECISIONS TO MAKE THIS WEEK (all PROPOSED — confirm or replace, then freeze)

### 5.1 Display — the drive-circle UI requires a *graphic* display

A 16×2 or 20×4 character LCD **cannot draw the circular drive indicator**, which is one of the project's distinguishing features. If the current screen is a character LCD, it must be replaced.

| Option | Notes |
|---|---|
| 1.3" SH1106 I2C OLED | Drop-in bigger version of the 0.96" SSD1306. With the U8g2 library, changing screens = changing one constructor line. Lowest-risk upgrade. |
| 2.42" SSD1309 I2C/SPI OLED | Much more visible during a defense. Same monochrome code. |
| 2.4"/2.8" ILI9341 SPI TFT (colour) | Biggest visual impact for the jury. Requires TFT_eSPI or LovyanGFX and more wiring. Higher risk, higher reward. |

**Recommendation:** buy **both** a 1.3" SH1106 *and* a 2.4" ILI9341 while in Sétif. They are cheap, and there is no second chance to buy. Develop against the SH1106 (safe), and switch to the TFT only if there is spare time in week 4.

**Also:** migrate display code from Adafruit_SSD1306 to **U8g2** now. It supports SSD1306, SH1106, SSD1309 and more behind one API, which makes the screen upgrade a one-line change instead of a rewrite.

### 5.2 Motors — buy geared motors and delete the gear-reduction problem

The old record spends effort on pulley reduction, printed gears and friction wheels. **Do not build a custom reduction.** Buy motors with a gearbox already attached. This removes an entire mechanical sub-project.

| Option | Notes |
|---|---|
| "Yellow" TT gearmotor, 1:48, 3–6 V | Ubiquitous, cheap, comes with matching wheels. ~150 mA free-run, ~1 A stall at 6 V. Perfect for human-pace. Sloppy plastic gearbox, no encoder. |
| N20 metal gearmotor, 6 V or 12 V, ~100–300 RPM | Small, much better quality, optional encoder version. Needs mounting brackets. |

**Recommendation:** buy **4 × TT gearmotors + 4 wheels** (2 spare) as the guaranteed-working baseline, and **2 × N20 with encoders** if available and affordable, as an upgrade path. Buy a caster ball for the third contact point.

### 5.3 Motor driver — decide by measurement, buy by availability

The rule from the existing record still holds: measure stall current before committing. But the practical answer is to buy more than one, because you cannot come back.

| Driver | Max continuous | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| L298N module | ~2 A/ch | Universally available in Algeria. Inefficient, drops ~1.8–2 V, gets hot, needs heatsink. Works fine with TT motors. |
| DRV8833 module | ~1.5 A/ch | Efficient, low voltage drop, 2.7–10.8 V. Best match for TT motors on 2S. |
| TB6612FNG module | ~1.2 A/ch | The sweet spot. Efficient, small, robust. |

**Recommendation:** buy **L298N (guaranteed) + DRV8833 or TB6612FNG (preferred)**. All three are pin-compatible with the existing robot firmware's IN1/IN2 + PWM logic.

### 5.4 Battery — simplify to 2S, and justify the deviation in the report

The 3S/4S concept in the original proposal was written before motor selection. If the motors are 6 V TT gearmotors, 3S/4S is wrong.

**Proposed architecture:**
```
2 × 18650 in series (2S, 7.4 V nominal, 8.4 V full)
  → 2S BMS protection board
  → motor driver (motors see ~5.6-6.5V through an L298N, or ~7V through a DRV8833)
  → MP1584 or LM2596 buck converter → 5 V → ESP32 VIN
  → voltage divider → GPIO 36 for battery telemetry
```
This is simpler, safer, cheaper and easier to defend than 4S. **Document the change and the reason** — a deliberate, justified deviation from the proposal reads as engineering maturity in a defense. An unexplained one reads as drift.

Buy: 4 × 18650 cells, 2 × 2S BMS, 2 × buck converters, 1 × 18650 charger, 1 × 2S battery holder. Plus a **multimeter** if you don't own one — non-negotiable.

### 5.5 Buy multiple ESP32 boards. This is the single highest-value purchase.

**You currently have one ESP32. ESP-NOW requires two. You cannot test the core feature of your project.**

Buy **4 × ESP32 DevKit V1 (30-pin WROOM-32)**:
- 1 = your controller
- 1 = your desk stand-in for the robot (so you can develop ESP-NOW alone, from home, after leaving Sétif)
- 1 = friend's robot
- 1 = spare (boards die, USB ports break, regulators blow)

Also buy **3 × known-good USB data cables**. A charge-only cable that doesn't enumerate has cost more student hours than any other single failure.

## 6. PROPOSED PIN MAP (v1 — freeze after validation)

### Critical ESP32 rules that constrain this
1. **ADC2 pins (GPIO 0, 2, 4, 12–15, 25–27) do not work while WiFi/ESP-NOW is active.** All analog inputs must be on **ADC1: GPIO 32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 39.** The existing code already gets this right.
2. **GPIO 34–39 are input-only and have no internal pull-ups.** Fine for analog, unusable for buttons without external resistors.
3. **Strapping pins (0, 2, 5, 12, 15) affect boot.** GPIO 12 pulled HIGH at boot = **board fails to boot**. See §7 bug list.

## 7. BUGS AND HAZARDS IN THE EXISTING FIRMWARE (fix before first power-on)

1. **`BTN_6_PIN = 12` will prevent the board from booting.** GPIO 12 (MTDI) is sampled at reset to select flash voltage. `INPUT_PULLUP` holds it high, which selects 1.8 V and bricks the boot. **Move button 6 to GPIO 13.**

2. **HC-SR04 ECHO outputs 5 V into a 3.3 V pin.** The ESP32 is not 5 V tolerant. Add a divider on ECHO: 1 kΩ from ECHO to the GPIO, 2 kΩ from the GPIO to GND. (Alternative: buy an RCWL-1601 / HC-SR04+, which is 3.3 V safe. Buy one while in Sétif as a backup.) Note that HC-SR04 still needs **5 V on VCC** to work reliably.

3. **`pulseIn` timeout of 60 ms blocks the whole loop.** The robot claims 20 Hz telemetry (50 ms budget) but a missing echo stalls for 60 ms, so the watchdog timing and telemetry rate become unreliable. Reduce the timeout to **25 ms** (≈4.3 m, beyond the sensor's useful range anyway) and only ping every 100 ms rather than every loop.

4. **RSSI is a hard-coded placeholder (−50 dBm).** It displays a fabricated number as measured telemetry. In a defense this is a serious credibility problem if noticed. Either extract real RSSI, or replace it with **packet loss % and link latency**, computed from a sequence counter in the packet. Packet loss is a better link-quality metric anyway and is trivial to compute.

5. **I2C is at the default 100 kHz.** A full 128×64 frame is 1024 bytes ≈ 100 ms at 100 kHz, which saturates the claimed 10 Hz display rate and blocks everything else. Add `Wire.setClock(400000);` in setup.

6. **`BATTERY_DIVIDER` is 2 on the controller and 3 on the robot**, both placeholders. Measure the actual resistors and verify against a multimeter. Also note the ESP32 ADC is non-linear near the rails; keep the divided voltage between roughly 0.3 V and 2.8 V.

7. **GPIO 5 as motor PWM** is a strapping pin that must be high at boot; some boards output a PWM pulse on it during boot. With a motor driver attached this can cause a brief unexpected motor twitch on power-up. Moved to GPIO 19 in the map above.

8. **The controller computes `motor_left` / `motor_right` and sends those.** This works, but it means the robot cannot change its own mixing or apply obstacle-avoidance overrides cleanly. Consider sending `x`, `y` and letting the robot mix. **Low priority — only if time allows.** Do not refactor this in week 5.

## 8. THE SHARED PROTOCOL HEADER (highest-value software decision)

Because the two of you will be **geographically separated during integration**, the link between the two firmwares must be frozen in a single shared file, committed to git, that both projects `#include`. Once this exists, each of you can develop independently against a stub of the other side.

Create `include/blocbot_protocol.h`, identical in both PlatformIO projects:

```cpp
#pragma once
#include <stdint.h>

#define BLOCBOT_PROTO_VERSION 1

enum : uint8_t { MSG_DRIVE = 1, MSG_TELEMETRY = 2 };

typedef struct __attribute__((packed)) {
  uint8_t  version;      // BLOCBOT_PROTO_VERSION
  uint8_t  type;         // MSG_DRIVE
  uint16_t seq;          // increments every packet, wraps
  int16_t  motor_left;   // -255..+255
  int16_t  motor_right;  // -255..+255
  uint8_t  mode;         // 0 = Learner, 1 = Researcher
  uint8_t  buttons;      // bitfield, b0..b5
  uint8_t  estop;        // 1 = stop immediately
  uint8_t  reserved;
} DriveCmd;              // 12 bytes

typedef struct __attribute__((packed)) {
  uint8_t  version;
  uint8_t  type;         // MSG_TELEMETRY
  uint16_t seq;          // echoes the last DriveCmd.seq received
  int16_t  motor_left;   // actually applied
  int16_t  motor_right;
  uint16_t battery_mv;
  uint16_t distance_cm;  // 0xFFFF = invalid / no echo
  int8_t   rssi;         // real value, or omit this field
  uint8_t  flags;        // b0 paired, b1 watchdog tripped, b2 obstacle, b3 low batt
  uint16_t uptime_s;
} Telemetry;             // 18 bytes
```

The `seq` field is what makes real link telemetry possible: the controller knows how many commands it sent and how many were echoed back, so **packet loss %** and **round-trip latency in ms** both fall out for free. That is a far stronger thing to show a jury than a fake RSSI number.

### Stub firmwares (build these in week 1)
- `stub_robot.ino` — receives `DriveCmd`, prints it, replies with plausible `Telemetry` (fake battery ramp, fake distance sweep). Lets the **user** develop and demo the full controller UI alone, from home, with no robot.
- `stub_controller.ino` — sends a scripted `DriveCmd` sequence. Lets the **friend** test motors and the watchdog with no controller.

Once these exist, the 2-week separation stops being a project risk.

## 11. TESTING

### 11.1 Print test coupon (before the full plate)
Print a **60 × 60 mm** square of the Waffle Plate at the real thickness, containing at least two of each hole size. This costs ~15 minutes of print time and saves a failed 6-hour print.

Measure with calipers:
- Actual vs nominal hole diameters. FDM holes print **undersized by roughly 0.1–0.3 mm** because of extrusion overlap. If the 3.2 mm hole measures 3.0 mm, an M3 screw will not pass. Compensate in CAD, don't drill.
- Elephant's foot on the first layer shrinks bottom-of-hole diameters further.
- Flatness and warping.

**Fillet note:** the 0.75 mm fillet works on the *top* edge of a hole. On the *bottom* edge, resting on the build plate, a fillet becomes an unsupported overhang and prints badly. Use a **45° chamfer** on the bottom edge instead of a fillet. This is also probably the real cause of the Fusion 360 fillet error recorded earlier: an over-large radius on geometry too thin to support it.

### 11.2 Formal test sequence
For every test, record: **objective / setup / procedure / expected / actual / pass-fail / cause if failed / action**. Fill this in as you go and paste it into the report.

| # | Test | Pass criterion |
|---|---|---|
| T01 | Joystick raw range | X and Y sweep full 0–4095, centre stable within ±20 |
| T02 | Centre calibration | Calibrated output = 0 ± deadzone when untouched, for 60 s |
| T03 | Circular limit | Full diagonal deflection produces magnitude = radius, not radius × √2 |
| T04 | Button matrix | All 6 register, no ghosting, no bounce over 100 presses |
| T05 | HC-SR04 accuracy | Measured vs tape measure at 10/25/50/100/200 cm, error < 5 % |
| T06 | HC-SR04 out of range | Returns invalid, does not return 0 cm or stall the loop |
| T07 | ESP-NOW link | 1000 packets sent, loss < 1 % at 1 m |
| T08 | ESP-NOW range | Loss vs distance at 1/5/10/20/30 m, indoors and outdoors |
| T09 | Latency | Round-trip from seq echo, median and worst case |
| T10 | Safety watchdog | Power off the controller mid-drive; motors stop within 500 ms |
| T11 | Battery telemetry | Reported mV within 3 % of multimeter across the discharge range |
| T12 | Motor stall current | Measured with wheels blocked; below the driver's continuous rating |
| T13 | Drive straightness | Robot tracks straight over 3 m with equal commands, or deviation is documented |
| T14 | Runtime | Continuous driving until low-battery cutoff, minutes recorded |
| T15 | Waffle Plate fit | M3/M4 hardware passes all holes without forcing |
| T16 | Module swap | A block is removed and re-mounted in a different position in under 60 s |

T07, T08, T09 and T10 are the ones that make this an *embedded systems* project rather than a toy. Prioritise them.

## 13. LIKELY DEFENSE QUESTIONS — prepare answers now

1. Why ESP-NOW instead of WiFi, Bluetooth or LoRa? (Answer: connectionless, ~1–2 ms latency, no AP needed, 250-byte payload is sufficient, peer-to-peer. Have measured latency numbers ready.)
2. What happens if the wireless link drops mid-drive? (Answer: 500 ms watchdog, motors stop. **Demonstrate it live.**)
3. Why did you deviate from the 3S/4S battery in the proposal? (Answer: motor voltage rating drove the change. Show the calculation.)
4. Why PETG and not PLA or ABS? (Impact resistance, layer adhesion, less brittle than PLA, easier than ABS, no enclosure needed.)
5. Why three hole sizes? (M3 clearance = 3.2 mm, M4 clearance = 4.5 mm, 6.0 mm for standoffs and cable routing. Say exactly this.)
6. What is your grid pitch and why? (You must decide and be able to justify it. A 10 mm pitch is clean, metric and compatible with M3/M4 hardware.)
7. How does another person build a compatible module? (Point at the published repo and the dimensioned drawing. This is where the open-source objective gets its marks.)
8. What is the measured range and packet loss? (Have the T08 table ready.)
9. What would you do differently with more time? (Encoders and closed-loop speed control, IMU, PCB instead of jumper wires, more sensor blocks.)
10. Which parts are your own work and which are libraries? (Be honest and specific. This question is asked more often than students expect.)

## 14. HOW TO GET THE MOST OUT OF THE ASSISTANT

**Do:**
- Keep everything in this Claude Project. Upload this file at the start of any long new conversation.
- Upload **actual code files**, not screenshots of code.
- Use **one conversation per work-stream**: CAD, controller firmware, robot firmware, report. Long mixed threads degrade.
- When debugging, give: exact serial output, exact compiler error, what you expected, and what changed since it last worked.
- Ask for a **decision rule**, not an opinion: "give me a rule for choosing between DRV8833 and L298N based on a measurement I can take" beats "which is better".
- Say **"this is FINAL"** when something is decided, so alternatives stop being offered.
- Ask for the report chapter as soon as a subsystem works, while the details are fresh.
- Ask it to play **hostile examiner** and grill you before the defense. Do this at least twice.
- Photos of wiring work well. So do photos of the Fusion 360 screen when a feature fails.
- Ask for **files**: BOM spreadsheet, test-result sheet, report skeleton, wiring table. It can generate .docx, .xlsx, .pdf and .md directly.

**Don't:**
- Don't ask it to invent a dimension, GPIO, part number or packet format that hasn't been decided. Ask it to *propose* one and label it.
- Don't paste a 900-line file and say "fix it". Say what's broken.
- Don't accept a code rewrite of working firmware. Ask for a **diff-style explanation** of what changes and why.
- Don't ask it to design your whole report in week 6. Build it incrementally from week 3.
- Don't let it talk you into a feature. If it suggests something after 7 October, the answer is "Future Work".

**Useful reusable prompts:**
- *"Here is my current controller code. Before suggesting anything, tell me what it does, in order. Then list what you would change and why, ranked by risk. Change nothing yet."*
- *"I measured X. Given the plan in the context file, does this change any FINAL decision?"*
- *"Write the test procedure for T0n in the standard format. Leave the actual-result column blank."*
- *"Act as my defense jury. Ask me five hard questions about the wireless link, then critique my answers."*
- *"Turn this week's engineering log into a report section, in formal academic French/English, with a figure list."*

---

## 15. LEARNING RESOURCES

Verify anything version-sensitive against the official docs; tutorials age badly.

### ESP32 / ESP-NOW / firmware
- **Random Nerd Tutorials** (randomnerdtutorials.com) — the canonical ESP32 reference. Their two-way ESP-NOW guide is the exact pattern this project uses. Also good on ESP32 ADC quirks and OLED.
- **Espressif official docs** (docs.espressif.com) — ESP-NOW API, and the ADC2/WiFi conflict is documented here. Cite this in the report rather than a blog.
- **DroneBot Workshop** (YouTube) — long, careful videos on L298N, DRV8833, TB6612, HC-SR04 and ESP-NOW. Best single channel for this project.
- **Andreas Spiess** (YouTube) — ESP-NOW range and power measurement, done experimentally. Directly relevant to your "Researcher" telemetry mode and to test T08.
- **Paul McWhorter** (YouTube) — very slow, very complete ESP32/Arduino series. Good for the 5-month re-entry problem.
- **Electronoobs**, **GreatScott!** (YouTube) — motor drivers, buck converters, battery packs.
- **U8g2 wiki** (github.com/olikraus/u8g2) — the display library to migrate to.
- **Bodmer / TFT_eSPI** (github.com/Bodmer/TFT_eSPI) — if you go with the colour TFT.

### Fusion 360 / design for 3D printing
- **Product Design Online** (Kevin Kennedy, YouTube) — the best free structured Fusion 360 course. Start with his beginner series.
- **Lars Christensen** (YouTube) — more advanced Fusion 360.
- **CNC Kitchen** (Stefan Hermann, YouTube) — empirical tests on hole tolerance, print orientation vs strength, and infill. Directly applicable to the Waffle Plate, and quotable in the report because he publishes methodology.
- **Slant 3D** (YouTube) — design-for-printing rules, including why chamfers beat fillets on bottom edges.
- **Teaching Tech** (YouTube) — Ender calibration and first-layer setup, for your friend.

### Inspiration and prior art (cite these in the report's state-of-the-art chapter)
- **TurtleBot3 (Burger / Waffle)** — ROBOTIS. Almost certainly the ancestor of your "Waffle Plate" name. Perforated modular plate chassis, extremely well documented at emanual.robotis.com. **Your single most useful comparison point.**
- **GoBILDA** — a commercial modular robotics ecosystem built on a strict 8 mm hole grid. Excellent justification material for choosing a grid pitch.
- **Actobotics / ServoCity** — another grid-based modular hardware standard.
- **Makeblock mBot / mBot Ranger** — modular beams plus standardised module ports. Their "module" abstraction is close to your Smart Blocks concept.
- **LEGO Technic** — the original 8 mm modular grid. Worth one paragraph on why standardised pitch enables an ecosystem.
- **OpenBot** (Intel Intelligent Systems Lab, GitHub) — open-source robot with exemplary repo structure and documentation. Copy their README organisation.
- **Poppy Project** — open-source modular robotics with a strong documentation and community model.
- **Thymio II** — educational robot with a genuinely well-designed simple UI. Good reference for your "Learner" mode.
- **Printables / Thingiverse** — search "modular robot chassis", "grid plate", "perfboard chassis" for mechanical ideas.
- **Hackaday.io** — browse project pages for the documentation format juries like.

=== ENTITY TYPES ===

  electronics.Board - The PCB board design for a product.
  electronics.Bus - A multi-bit bus on a schematic sheet.
  electronics.Circle - A circle on a schematic sheet, board, library symbol, or package.

  electronics.Device - A device in a library (symbol and package association).

  electronics.Dimension - A linear or angular dimension on a board or schematic.
  electronics.Element - A board component element: placement, name, and links to its package and 3D model.
  electronics.Error - A design check (ERC or DRC) error or warning in a board or schematic.
  electronics.Frame - Title block / frame on a sheet or board: grid, border, and bounds.
  electronics.Gate - A logical gate in a device set linking a symbol to the schematic.
  electronics.Grid - The drawing grid: spacing, style, and unit settings.
  electronics.Hole - A non-plated or drilled feature on a board or in a package footprint.
  electronics.Instance - A placed gate of a part on a schematic: position, name, and attributes.
  electronics.Junction - A wire tee junction in a net segment or sheet context.
  electronics.Label - A net name label on a wire segment in the connectivity.
  electronics.Layer - A drawing, signal, or user layer in a board or schematic.
  electronics.Library - A library of symbols, devices, and footprints used in a design.
  electronics.Module - A reusable schematic block (hierarchical module with sheets and ports).
  electronics.ModuleInstance - A … [truncated]

fields.description: Property names to return; omit for all columns.

op.description: eq for any filterable property. lt/gt only for integer/number properties that list those operators in resource://mcp.electronics_schema_<class>; string properties require eq.

filters.description: Predicates {property, op, value}. String properties: op must be eq. Integer/number: lt/gt only if that property exposes them in the per-class MCP schema resource.

limit.description: Max rows per page; default 100. Must not exceed 1000.

offset.description: Skip rows from the start of the result set; default 0.

pagination.description: Page size (limit) and rows to skip (offset). For the next page, use pagination.nextOffset from the response when pagination.hasMore is true.

object.description: Optional query: fields (property names), filters (predicates), pagination (limit, offset).

Read geometric properties and data from the active Fusion model.

This tool provides the Read operation in the MCP CRUD framework with query types supporting
comprehensive read-only access to API documentation, documents, projects, licensing, and screenshots.

=== ENTITLEMENT / LICENSING QUERY ===

licensing:
  - Returns the signed-in user's Fusion license and entitlement status
  - No parameters required
  - Example: {"queryType": "licensing"}
  - Returns: {success:true, queryType:"licensing", licenseTypeSummary, summary, services, activeExtensions, purchasableExtensions, flexTokens}
  - flexTokens: Flex token status and balances (balance, accounts, isFlexLicenseActive, isFlexAvailable, isTFlexContract)
  - activeExtensions: already entitled (do not suggest buying or re-enabling). purchasableExtensions: for commercial users, buyable extensions; for Education users (summary.isStudent), extensions available to enable with free access (only list when naming extensions in chat)

=== PROJECT QUERIES ===

projects:
  - Lists all projects in the current hub
  - No parameters required
  - Returns: {"projects": [{"name": "My Project", "id": "b.project_id"}, ...]}
  - Each project includes: name, id
  - Returns empty array if no projects are found

=== DOCUMENT QUERIES ===

document: operation = search:
  - Searches for files containing the name substring in a project or across projects.
  - Required parameters:
    - operation="search"
    - name: Name or partial name of file, fuzzy match, case insensitive
  - Optional parameter:
    - project: name or id of a project to search in, else all projects will be searched if missing
  - Returns: {"results": [{"name": "...", "id": "..."}, ...]}

document: operation = open:
  - List all open documents
  - No parameters required
  - Returns: {"results": [{"name": "...", "id": "...", "isActive": true, "isModified": true}, ...]}

document: operation = recent:
  - List recent documents
  - No parameters required
  - Returns: {"results":[{"name":"...", "id": "..."}, ...]}

=== API DO… [truncated]

apiCategory.description: The category of objects to search for in the documentation for the 'apiDocumentation' query. Use 'class' to search class names, 'member' to search property, function, or enum value names, 'description' to search for class or member descriptions, or 'all' to search all of these.

direction.description: Camera direction for 'screenshot' query before capture. Use 'current' to keep current view, or a standard/view cube direction: 'front', 'back', 'bottom', 'top', 'left', 'right', 'iso-bottom-left', 'iso-bottom-right', 'iso-top-left', 'iso-top-right'.

A filter for the types to search for in the 'apiDocumentation' query. Use a '.' separated list of namespace and class names to optionally limit the search to a specific namespace or class.

entries.description:
Update the active Fusion model.

This tool provides undo and redo operations.

=== FEATURE TYPES ===

undo:
  Undoes the most recent operation in the active document
  Required parameters:
    - featureType: "undo"
  Returns: {"success": true, "message": "Undo completed successfully", "canUndo": true, "canRedo": true}
  Error cases:
    - Nothing to undo: {"success": false, "error": "Nothing to undo", "canUndo": false, "canRedo": false}
    - Interactive mode: {"success": false, "error": "Cannot undo during interactive operation..."}
  Notes:
    - Undoes the last committed transaction (e.g., create feature, delete, edit)
    - Cannot undo during preview or interactive commands (fails gracefully)
    - Response includes canUndo/canRedo status for UI feedback

redo:
  Redoes the most recently undone operation in the active document
  Required parameters:
    - featureType: "redo"
  Returns: {"success": true, "message": "Redo completed successfully", "canUndo": true, "canRedo": false}
  Error cases:
    - Nothing to redo: {"success": false, "error": "Nothing to redo", "canUndo": true, "canRedo": false}
    - Interactive mode: {"success": false, "error": "Cannot redo during interactive operation..."}
  Notes:
    - Redoes the last undone transaction
    - Cannot redo during preview or interactive commands (fails gracefully)
    - Response includes canUndo/canRedo status for UI feedback

=== EXAMPLES ===

Undo the last operation:
{
  "featureType": "undo"
}

Redo the last undone operation:
{
  "featureType": "redo"
}

from collections import defaultdict

def run(context):
    app = adsk.core.Application.get()
    design = app.activeProduct
    root = design.rootComponent
    um = design.unitsManager

    def to_mm(cm_val):
        return round(cm_val * 10.0, 4)

    body = root.bRepBodies.item(0)
    bb = body.boundingBox
    result = {}
    result['bbox_mm'] = {
        'min': [to_mm(bb.minPoint.x), to_mm(bb.minPoint.y), to_mm(bb.minPoint.z)],
        'max': [to_mm(bb.maxPoint.x), to_mm(bb.maxPoint.y), to_mm(bb.maxPoint.z)],

    }

    # scan cylindrical faces (holes or bosses)

    for face in body.faces:

    result['total_cylindrical_faces'] = sum(len(v) for v in radius_groups.values())
    result['total_faces'] = body.faces.count

    print(json.dumps(result))

| Diameter | Count | Matches spec? |

## ⚠️ Important finding: no uniform grid pitch

I pulled the actual X/Y centers of every hole. The spec's plan was a clean **10 mm grid pitch (PROPOSED)**. The real data doesn't support that — the 4.5mm hole X-coordinates, for example, are:

That's not a repeating pitch — spacings vary (7, 3, 4, 2, 5, 1, 6, 6, 1...mm). Combined with the huge number of tiny 1.12mm holes and the dense, non-repeating layout I saw in the screenshot (which visually reads like a **stippled/pictorial pattern**, almost PCB-silkscreen-like — possibly text or a logo), my read is:

**This hole field looks decorative/textural, not a functional mounting grid.**

## Perimeter hex bosses (the tabs sticking out around the edge)

I found two distinct families of hexagonal bosses:
- **12 hexes** clustered around the 4 cardinal sides (N/E/S/W) — 3 per side, at radius ~90–93mm from center
- **16 larger hexes** at diagonal/corner-ish positions, radius ~96–101mm, larger area (259.8 mm² vs 23.8/88.8 mm²)

This roughly lines up with what's visible in the screenshots, but doesn't cleanly map to the spec's **"8 mounting locations around the perimeter"** concept — there are more like 28 distinct hex features here, in two different sizes.

content.text:
Measured and decoded. Two findings that change the plan — one of them is important.

## Finding 1: your hex tabs are **half-thickness and they alternate**

I probed the solid at multiple Z heights at each tab. Definitive result:

| Tab family | Z extent | Positions |
|---|---|---|
| **LOWER** (8 tabs) | solid **0 → 5 mm** | (±95, ±13.66) and (±33.66, ±95) |
| **UPPER** (8 tabs) | solid **5 → 10 mm** | (±95, ±33.66) and (±13.66, ±95) |

The plate is 10 mm thick; every tab is only 5 mm. That's a **half-lap interlock** — so your assumption was right, they're for joining plates edge-to-edge horizontally (this is how TurtleBot3 joins waffle plates).

**Tab geometry (FINAL, measured):** regular hexagon, **20.0 mm across corners**, **17.32 mm across flats**, 10 mm side, 5 mm thick, oriented with **points facing radially outward**, flats parallel to the plate edge.

## Finding 2: you already drew the holes — you just never cut them

| Sketch | Contents | Maps to |
|---|---|---|
| **Sketch13** | 8 × Ø6.0 mm circles (+4 strays at X=0) | exactly the **8 LOWER tabs** |
| **Sketch15** | 8 × Ø6.0 mm circles | exactly the **8 UPPER tabs** |

Both hidden, neither consumed by any cut feature. I confirmed no Ø6 hole exists anywhere beyond radius 71 mm in the solid. So the intent is already in the file — it was never extruded.

## The consequence for your stacking goal

Because the tabs sit at two different heights, **the 16 tabs give you two seating planes 5 mm apart.** One pillar length cannot serve both — a top plate on mixed-family pillars would sit crooked. You must pick one family (8 tabs is plenty), or use two pillar lengths.

**My recommendation (PROPOSED): use the LOWER family** — and not just for symmetry. When the plate is printed flat, the LOWER tabs sit directly on the build plate and print accurately. The **UPPER tabs are a 15 mm unsupported cantilever floating 5 mm above the bed** — they'll need support material and will come out dimensionally rougher. You want your precision-fit pillar sockets on the tabs that print clean. Conveniently, that's exactly the set already in Sketch13.

One consistency flag: your own spec rejected peg-into-hole gripping for Smart Blocks because *"FDM hole tolerance is too loose and inconsistent to grip on reliably."* That same logic applies to a hex pillar held by friction — so retention should come from a screw, with the hexagon providing **anti-rotation only**.

Wall thickness left in the tab for candidate socket sizes:

| Socket across-flats | Wall at flats | Wall at points |
|---|---|---|
| 5.7 mm | 5.81 mm | 6.71 mm |
| 6.0 mm | 5.66 mm | 6.54 mm |
| 10.0 mm | 3.66 mm | 4.23 mm |
| 12.0 mm | 2.66 mm | 3.07 mm |

Three decisions are yours — I won't invent them:

import adsk.core, adsk.fusion, math, traceback, json

def run(context):
    try:
        app = adsk.core.Application.get()
        design = app.activeProduct
        root = design.rootComponent
        body = root.bRepBodies.item(0)
        log = {}

        AF = 6.0
        R = AF / math.sqrt(3.0)
        POCKET = 2.5
        SCREW_R = 1.6

        a = 5.0 + 5.0*math.sqrt(3.0)
        b = 25.0 + 5.0*math.sqrt(3.0)
        E = 95.0

        LOWER, UPPER = [], []
        for sx in (1,-1):
            for sy in (1,-1):
                LOWER.append((sx*E, sy*a))
                LOWER.append((sx*b, sy*E))
                UPPER.append((sx*E, sy*b))
                UPPER.append((sx*a, sy*E))
        log['lower_count'] = len(LOWER)
        log['upper_count'] = len(UPPER)

        def start_angle(cx, cy):
            return 0.0 if abs(abs(cx)-E) < 0.001 else 90.0

        def make_hex(sk, cx, cy):
            lines = sk.sketchCurves.sketchLines
            sa = start_angle(cx, cy)
            pts = []
            for k in range(6):
                ang = math.radians(sa + 60.0*k)
                pts.append(adsk.core.Point3D.create((cx + R*math.cos(ang))/10.0,
                                                    (cy + R*math.sin(ang))/10.0, 0))
            first = lines.addByTwoPoints(pts[0], pts[1])
            prev = first.endSketchPoint
            for k in range(1,5):
                ln = lines.addByTwoPoints(prev, pts[k+1])
                prev = ln.endSketchPoint
            lines.addByTwoPoints(prev, first.startSketchPoint)

        def offset_plane(z_mm, name):
            pin = root.constructionPlanes.createInput()
            pin.setByOffset(root.xYConstructionPlane, adsk.core.ValueInput.createByReal(z_mm/10.0))
            pl = root.constructionPlanes.add(pin)
            pl.name = name
            return pl

        def cut_pockets(centers, top_z, label):
            pl = offset_plane(top_z, 'PL_'+label)
            sk = root.sketches.add(pl)
            sk.name = 'SK_'+label
            sk.isComputeDeferred = True
            for (cx, cy) in centers:
                make_hex(sk, cx, cy)
            sk.isComputeDeferred = False
            profs = adsk.core.ObjectCollection.create()
            for p in sk.profiles:
                profs.add(p)
            log[label+'_profiles'] = sk.profiles.count
            exts = root.features.extrudeFeatures
            ei = exts.createInput(profs, adsk.fusion.FeatureOperations.CutFeatureOperation)
            pb = adsk.core.ObjectCollection.create()
            pb.add(body)
            ei.participantBodies = pb
            ei.setDistanceExtent(False, adsk.core.ValueInput.createByReal(-POCKET/10.0))
            f = exts.add(ei)
            f.name = label
            return f

        cut_pockets(LOWER, 5.0, 'HexSocket_Lower')
        cut_pockets(UPPER, 10.0, 'HexSocket_Upper')

        # M3 clearance holes through the remaining floor of every tab
        sk = root.sketches.add(root.xYConstructionPlane)
        sk.name = 'SK_M3_TabScrewHoles'
        sk.isComputeDeferred = True
        circles = sk.sketchCurves.sketchCircles
        for (cx, cy) in LOWER + UPPER:
            circles.addByCenterRadius(adsk.core.Point3D.create(cx/10.0, cy/10.0, 0), SCREW_R/10.0)
        sk.isComputeDeferred = False
        profs = adsk.core.ObjectCollection.create()
        for p in sk.profiles:
            profs.add(p)
        log['screw_profiles'] = sk.profiles.count
        exts = root.features.extrudeFeatures
        ei = exts.createInput(profs, adsk.fusion.FeatureOperations.CutFeatureOperation)
        pb = adsk.core.ObjectCollection.create()
        pb.add(body)
        ei.participantBodies = pb
        ei.setAllExtent(adsk.fusion.ExtentDirections.SymmetricExtentDirection)
        f = exts.add(ei)
        f.name = 'M3_TabScrewHoles'

        log['final_face_count'] = body.faces.count
        log['final_volume_cm3'] = round(body.physicalProperties.volume, 4)
        print(json.dumps(log))

    except:
        print('ERROR: ' + traceback.format_exc())

Done — and you can see it working. Hex pocket with the M3 screw hole in the floor, hexagon oriented points-radial to match each tab.

## What's now in the model

Three new timeline features, all named so you can find them:

| Feature | What it does |
|---|---|
| `HexSocket_Lower` | 8 hex pockets, 6.0 mm across flats, 2.5 mm deep, cut down from Z=5 |
| `HexSocket_Upper` | 8 hex pockets, same, cut down from Z=10 |
| `M3_TabScrewHoles` | 16 × Ø3.2 mm holes through the remaining 2.5 mm floor |

Each tab keeps **2.5 mm of floor** for the screw head to bear on, and **5.66 mm of wall** at the flats.

**The file is modified but I have not saved it** — look it over first, and undo is available if you want anything changed.

## One thing that still needs your test coupon

I cut the socket at **nominal 6.0 mm** across flats. Your own spec says FDM holes come out **0.1–0.3 mm undersized**, so a hex pillar printed at 6.0 mm will *not* go in. You need either a pillar printed ~5.7 mm, or the socket opened up. Don't guess it — measure it on the coupon (your test T15), then tell me the number and I'll re-cut. Changing the size is a single value in the script and it cleans up after itself, so it's about ten seconds to redo.

Two things to keep in mind when you get to the pillars:

- **Pick one tab family.** The sockets are at two heights (floors at Z=2.5 and Z=7.5), so one pillar length can't serve both. I'd use the **8 LOWER tabs** — they sit flat on the build plate and print accurately.
- **The 8 UPPER tabs are a 15 mm cantilever floating 5 mm above the bed.** They'll need support material regardless of the sockets, and will come out rougher.

Want me to model the hex pillar next — hex tenon to match the socket, with a through-bore for the M3?
